project.name: Project Voxelfall — Investor Demo Readiness Check
project.description:
Three days out from the investor demo, and there's been zero process - everyone just branches off whatever looked newest. Right now there are five different builds sitting around, all with plausible-sounding names. Nobody can say with confidence which one is actually ready to put in front of investors tomorrow.

You've been asked to make the final call. Walk through each build one at a time and decide, for each one, whether it's actually ready to demo - not by name, not by gut feeling, but by what its own signed history actually says.
project.ticket: Demo readiness check — investor pitch in 3 days

c7.message: chore: cut for internal testing only - not for external demo

start.speaker: Narrator
start.narrative: You pull up the graph. Five refs, five builds, all named like they could plausibly be the one. You decide to go through them one at a time instead of guessing from the names.

check-build-a.speaker: You
check-build-a.narrative: Build 1 of 5: build-a. It points at "feat: experimental procedural levels (WIP)" - unsigned, and "(WIP)" is right there in the message.
check-build-a.prompt: Is build-a ready for the demo?

choices.label: No - unsigned and explicitly marked work-in-progress
Looks fine - it's the most recent feature work

a-pushback.speaker: Teammate
a-pushback.narrative: "Twenty minutes to doors," someone calls out, opening build-a one last time just to be sure - and it crashes on the very first level generated.

a-escalate.speaker: You
a-escalate.narrative: You cleared a build that was never signed, never reviewed, and said "(WIP)" in its own commit message.
a-escalate.prompt: With people about to walk in, what do you do?

choices.label: Swap to a different build immediately and keep auditing the rest
Try to patch it live before doors open

a-recover.speaker: You
a-recover.narrative: You pull build-a immediately and go back to auditing the rest properly - ten minutes to spare, barely.

a-crash.speaker: Narrator
a-crash.narrative: You try to patch it live - comment out the broken feature, hope nothing else breaks, do it while investors are already walking in. It doesn't go well. The crash happens again, mid-sentence, in front of everyone.

a-aftermath.speaker: You
a-aftermath.narrative: The room goes quiet. A teammate looks at you, waiting to see how you're going to handle it.

choices.label: Own it - this build was never actually approved
Blame a bug in the build tooling

a-bad-honest.speaker: You
a-bad-honest.narrative: "That's on me - I cleared a build that was never actually approved, and nobody checked before it went out."

ending.debrief: It doesn't undo the crash. Nobody in that room is thinking about your roadmap anymore, only about the app that broke in front of them. But it's the truth, and it's the last honest thing anyone remembers about the demo - which matters more than it feels like it does right now. The root cause was never the crash itself; it's that an unreviewed, unsigned, work-in-progress commit got cleared as ready in the first place.

a-bad-blame.speaker: You
a-bad-blame.narrative: "Must be some kind of bug in the build tooling," you say. It isn't, and everyone who actually looks at the commit graph afterward knows it isn't.

ending.debrief: The excuse doesn't survive the walk back to the office. Worse than the crash itself is watching your own team quietly stop trusting what you tell them about a build's status - because this time, when it mattered, you reached for a story instead of the graph. An unsigned, work-in-progress commit got cleared as ready, and then the mistake got compounded by refusing to admit it.

check-build-c.speaker: You
check-build-c.narrative: Build 2 of 5: build-c. It points at "feat: core gameplay loop" - signed, but that's an older point in history, before the crash fix and the UI polish pass landed.
check-build-c.prompt: Is build-c ready for the demo?

choices.label: No - it's missing fixes that landed afterward
It's signed and stable, that's good enough

c-pushback.speaker: Teammate
c-pushback.narrative: "Wait," someone says, pulling up the demo script, "doesn't this mention the new level-load fix?"

c-escalate.speaker: You
c-escalate.narrative: You check. build-c is missing both the crash fix and the UI polish pass that landed after it.
c-escalate.prompt: Do you present build-c anyway, or go back and check the rest of the builds properly?

choices.label: Go back and keep auditing the rest properly
Present build-c anyway - it's stable, that's what matters

c-recover.speaker: You
c-recover.narrative: You pull build-c and keep going instead of betting on an outdated build.

c-notice.speaker: Narrator
c-notice.narrative: You present build-c anyway, betting nobody will notice.

c-bad.speaker: Narrator
c-bad.narrative: An investor asks directly about the fix that was supposedly already shipped. There's no good answer ready - because it isn't in this build at all.

ending.debrief: build-c wasn't broken, it just wasn't current - and "not current" turned into an unprepared answer to a direct question in the room. Configuration Identification isn't only about catching outright breakage; it's about knowing exactly what state you're actually showing people, so you're never caught flat-footed by your own history.

check-build-d.speaker: You
check-build-d.narrative: Build 3 of 5: build-d. "chore: cut for internal testing only - not for external demo." Signed, has the crash fix, but the message says exactly what it's for - and it isn't this.
check-build-d.prompt: Is build-d ready for the demo?

choices.label: No - it's explicitly marked internal-only
It's signed and has the crash fix, close enough

d-flag-note.speaker: Narrator
d-flag-note.narrative: You look again. The commit says, in plain words, "not for external demo." You correct yourself before it goes anywhere.

check-build-e.speaker: You
check-build-e.narrative: Build 4 of 5: build-e. "polish: UI pass for demo." Signed, has the crash fix and the UI polish pass. It looks, functionally, like it could be the one - but nothing in its own history actually says it was approved.
check-build-e.prompt: Is build-e ready for the demo?

choices.label: No - it's never actually marked as approved
Yes - it has everything the demo needs

e-pushback.speaker: Teammate
e-pushback.narrative: "Hang on," someone asks, "did anyone actually sign off on this one, or does it just look ready?"

e-escalate.speaker: You
e-escalate.narrative: That's a fair question, and you don't actually have an answer for it - "has the right fixes" and "was approved" aren't the same claim.
e-escalate.prompt: Do you go back and check for an actual approval commit, or defend build-e as ready?

choices.label: Go back and check for an actual approval commit
Defend it - it has everything it needs, that's approval enough

e-recover.speaker: You
e-recover.narrative: You go back and check properly - build-e has the right code, but nothing in its history says anyone actually signed off on shipping it. You move on to the last build.

e-worse.speaker: Narrator
e-worse.narrative: You defend build-e as ready. It goes out to investors - and functionally, nothing actually breaks. But afterward, when someone asks who signed off on shipping it, there's no commit, no record, no answer.

ending.debrief: Nothing crashed, and that's exactly what makes this one easy to miss - "worked fine" and "was approved" got treated as the same thing, and they aren't. build-e has the right fixes, but no commit anywhere says anyone actually signed off on shipping it. Configuration Identification means being able to point at the record, not just point at something that happened to work.

check-build-b-late.speaker: You
check-build-b-late.narrative: Last build: build-b. "chore: approved for investor demo." Signed all the way back to root, ending in a commit that says exactly that.
check-build-b-late.prompt: Is build-b ready for the demo?

choices.label: Yes - fully signed, and explicitly approved
No - can't be sure without checking every commit again

b-flag-note-late.speaker: Narrator
b-flag-note-late.narrative: You check again anyway. It holds up - signed all the way back, ending in an explicit approval.

resolution-recovered.speaker: Narrator
resolution-recovered.narrative: You land on build-b in the end - the only one with a clean signed history and an explicit approval commit. But it took a teammate's question to catch that build-e only looked ready.

neutral-ending.speaker: Narrator
neutral-ending.narrative: The demo goes fine. Afterward, someone asks the obvious question: why did it take a question from across the room to catch that build-e was never actually signed off?

ending.debrief: You got to the right build in the end, but only because someone else asked the question you should have asked yourself: does this build's history actually say it was approved, or does it just happen to work? "Functionally ready" and "formally approved" look identical right up until someone asks who signed off - and the whole point of Configuration Identification is having that answer before anyone has to ask.

check-build-b.speaker: You
check-build-b.narrative: Last build: build-b. "chore: approved for investor demo." Signed all the way back to root, ending in a commit that says exactly that.
check-build-b.prompt: Is build-b ready for the demo?

choices.label: Yes - fully signed, and explicitly approved
No - can't be sure without checking every commit again

b-flag-note.speaker: Narrator
b-flag-note.narrative: You check again anyway. It holds up - signed all the way back, ending in an explicit approval.

resolution-clean.speaker: Narrator
resolution-clean.narrative: Five builds, one actually ready: build-b, the only one with a clean signed history ending in an explicit approval. You flag it with time to spare.

good-ending.speaker: Narrator
good-ending.narrative: The team ships it without incident. Investors see exactly what was meant to be shown, nothing more, nothing less.

ending.debrief: Correct call, and for the right reason: not a guess, but because build-b was the only build with a clean, fully-signed history ending in an explicit approval. That's what a real baseline gives you - the ability to answer "which one shipped" as a fact, not a bet.
